newsitem.title: FRANCE: Saab profit may be 18 months away.
newsitem.headline: Saab profit may be 18 months away.

text.p: Swedish car maker Saab Automobile will not break even this year and may not make a profit in 1997, Chief Executive Officer Robert Hendry said Monday.
"We will not reach breakeven this year. There is also a question about next year. Profit may be 18 months away," Hendry said in an interview.
Saab is owned 50-50 by General Motors Corp. and the Investor group. Its results have been weighed down by big investments in product development and a rise in the Swedish currency, Hendry said.

"My mandate from GM and Investor on being named CEO of Saab Automobile was of course to turn the company into a profitable one. The number of years was not qualified but GM will not be patient forever. In the next two, three years we must turn Saab Automobile around," Hendry said.
Saab Automobile aims to sell 150,000 cars by the year 2000. In 1995 sales amounted to 98,700.

"Saab Automobile will remain a niche player but what our exact size will be in the future I am not sure. I do not know the potential once we reach our goal of selling 150,000 cars a year. It may be 200,000 cars a year, maybe more," Hendry said.
He said the goal of reaching sales of 150,000 cars a year by 2000 was both feasible and possible.

A key element in making the group profitable again is to make it more customer-oriented and strengthen the Saab identity -- a car for independent thinkers offering high performance, security and intelligent technology, Hendry said.
Saab also needs to cut costs further. One way to do that is to increase the number of GM components in future Saab models.

"We can neutralise our small production size by leveraging GM and that in more ways than one. Components, yes, but also marketing, parts sales and tapping into GM's worldwide organisation. We can do that while still keeping a Saab a Saab," Hendry said.
In the future Saab plans to have two models -- the 900 and a new 640 sedan to be introduced in 1997. The 9000 will be discontinued.
"The new 640 is to replace the 9000 model. Saab 640 will, together with the 900 series, become our two mainstream models," Hendry said.
Saab will also add a diesel engine to its product line within the next couple of years, he added.
